new_entities.name: Low-dose aspirin for recurrent miscarriage
aliases: baby aspirin for recurrent pregnancy loss
low-dose aspirin in recurrent spontaneous abortion
new_entities.description: Use of low-dose aspirin, usually alone or as part of antithrombotic therapy, in women with recurrent miscarriage or recurrent pregnancy loss.

new_entities.name: Live birth rate
new_entities.description: The probability of delivering a live infant after a fertility treatment cycle or conception attempt.

edges.effect_quant: The strongest quantitative takeaway is that low-dose aspirin alone does not reliably improve live birth in antiphospholipid-related recurrent loss. In a 1,251-patient meta-analysis, aspirin alone versus placebo showed no live-birth benefit (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.16), whereas heparin-containing regimens performed better.
edges.population: women with recurrent miscarriage or recurrent pregnancy loss, especially those with antiphospholipid antibodies or antiphospholipid syndrome
edges.mechanism: Aspirin may reduce platelet activation and placental microthrombotic risk, which is why it is biologically attractive in antiphospholipid-associated pregnancy loss. The clinical reality is that aspirin alone often underperforms, and any meaningful benefit appears more tied to combined anticoagulant strategies than to aspirin monotherapy itself.
edges.summary: This is not a cleanly protective aspirin edge. The evidence supports a mixed conclusion: low-dose aspirin alone is usually not enough to improve live birth, while better outcomes are more often seen when heparin is part of the regimen in selected APS populations.
edges.caveats: This literature is highly subgroup-dependent. Findings in persistent antiphospholipid-antibody syndromes should not be generalized to all recurrent-loss populations, and this edge should not be upgraded on the basis of combination therapy results alone.

evidence.citation: HamulyákEN et al 2020 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
evidence.notes: Aspirin or heparin or both for improving pregnancy outcomes in women with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies and recurrent pregnancy loss.
